title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Mill and Its Currents

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to live inside one of the great novels of the nineteenth century.
George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss — published in 1860 — is a novel about a river, a family, and a girl who is too large for the world she's given.
It is also, quietly, one of the most devastating social anatomies in the English language.
Today, in this opening episode, we're asking a simple question: what kind of world does Maggie Tulliver inhabit, and what does it cost her?
To help me think through that, I have three brilliant readers with me — and I should introduce them properly.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he is going to keep us honest about who benefits and who pays in this world Eliot has built.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong Tory who believes the novel's genius lies in moral imagination — character tested by circumstance, not social programme.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite let go of it — she'll make sure we remember what it actually feels like on the page.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because you've brought us a character who, in some ways, embodies everything about the world Maggie is born into.
Thank you — and yes, I think the Reverend Walter Stelling is as fine a comic creation as Eliot ever produced.
He arrives in the novel broad-chested, flaxen-haired, with — as Eliot puts it — an air of defiant self-confidence inclining to brazenness.
And what Eliot is doing — with exquisite precision — is showing us a man who has perfectly mastered the appearances of merit without possessing the substance.
The preaching style he has chosen is the extemporaneous — held, she tells us, as little short of the miraculous in rural parishes.
He recycles passages of Massillon and Bourdaloue from memory, and his own comparatively feeble appeals, delivered in the same loud and impressive manner, were often thought quite as striking.
The satire is perfectly calibrated — it never tips into caricature.
And then she gives us this sentence, which I consider a minor masterpiece of ironic logic.
"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting."
That word naturally — doing so much quiet, devastating work.
Stelling's debt is not a moral failing — it is, by the logic of his world, almost a duty.
What I love about that passage is the rhythm of the argument Eliot constructs inside Stelling's own head.
The furniture must be purchased, the wine laid in, the flower-garden laid out — and either these things are procured by other means, or Stelling must go without them.
Which last alternative, Eliot says drily, would be an absurd procrastination of the fruits of success, where success was certain.
It reads almost like a syllogism — and then you realise the syllogism is entirely corrupt.
But why it matters for Maggie — and this is what I keep returning to — is that this is the man into whose hands her brother Tom's education is placed.
Stelling's vanity and self-deception ripple outward and shape the children.
I think Edmund and Caroline are both right about the comedy — but I want to name what the comedy is actually doing.
Stelling is not an anomaly — he is the system working exactly as designed.
His doctrine is of no particular school — if anything, it had a tinge of evangelicalism, because that was, in Eliot's own phrase, the telling thing just then in the diocese.
Market logic applied to the Church of England.
And the people who bear the cost of Stelling's ambition — the children he badly educates, the labourers who service his superior flower-garden — they don't appear in his calculations at all.
I don't entirely disagree with Daniel — though I'd resist the tidiness of that verdict.
What makes Stelling rich as a character is precisely that he is not a villain.
He is a man of genuine good spirits who is utterly unexamined — which Eliot finds, I think, more troubling than malice.
Now — what brings me to this opening conversation with some urgency — is that we see what all this confident, unreflective self-advancement produces in a child like Maggie.
Eliot gives us a passage of extraordinary tenderness — Maggie rushing upstairs, the tears coming, and then this.
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
That phrase — the soul is made up of wants — stops me every time.
It is the most precise description I know of what adolescence actually is — not a stage, but a condition of exposure.
That sentence undoes me every time I read it.
And notice what comes just before it — Maggie thinking about books.
In books there were people who were always agreeable or tender, and delighted to do things that made one happy.
Maggie's entire inner world has been formed by reading — and then reality refuses to match it.
And Eliot doesn't condescend to her for that.
That parenthetical — though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair — that's Eliot turning to face us directly, indicting the reader.
We have the vision of the future that Maggie lacks — and we use it to dismiss her suffering.
Caroline has identified something vital — the narrator's refusal to let us off the hook.
But I want to push a little further into the material conditions of that suffering.
Eliot doesn't let us forget what Maggie's alternative actually is — poverty and the companionship of her mother's narrow griefs.
Those words — narrow griefs — are quietly brutal.
Mrs Tulliver's suffering is not small — it has simply been compressed by circumstance into a shape that looks small.
And Maggie can already see the trajectory — that this may be her life too.
And there is a third passage I want to bring in — because it shows us Maggie several years on, and the suffering has not lessened; if anything, it has found new channels.
She has attempted what I can only call a spiritual project — a withdrawal from desire, an ascent to what she imagines as serene heights above worldly conflict.
And she believes she has succeeded — for a time.
Then comes this passage, which Eliot writes with real force.
"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict.
And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions."
Down again — two words, and they carry the weight of the whole novel's argument about renunciation.
The heights were always a consolation, never a permanent home.
What hits me in that passage is the physical specificity at the end.
Maggie isn't just distressed in some vague, novelistic way.
Eliot tells us her heart bled for Philip, and the recollection of the insults flung at him was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her.
"Making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm."
That image — the foot, the palm — is almost unbearable in its exactness.
Empathy, for Maggie, is not a feeling — it is a physical event.
And it's Philip she is suffering for — Philip Wakem, the son of the man who holds the Tulliver family in legal bondage.
Maggie's empathy crosses the very line that the social order has drawn to divide her family from his.
Which is why Tom's cruelty toward Philip is not simply Tom being unkind — it is Tom enforcing a boundary the system requires.
And Maggie's penitence and submission are obstructed, Eliot says, by resentment that presents itself to her as just indignation.
She is right to be angry — and she knows it — and that clarity is precisely what makes her dangerous to everyone around her.
Dangerous — and yet so entirely alone with that clarity.
I think that's exactly the tension this novel is going to keep pulling on — the gap between what Maggie understands and what her world will allow her to say or do with that understanding.
We've had Stelling's ambition, Maggie's grief, and the first glimpse of how empathy itself becomes a source of suffering in this novel.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the landscape itself — the river, the mill, the town of St Ogg's — and ask what kind of weight the physical world carries in Eliot's imagination.

segments.title: Class, Capital, and the Tulliver Collapse

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into the engine room of the novel — the economic ruin of the Tullivers, and what that collapse reveals about class, pride, and the brutal logic of Victorian commercial life.
With me are three readers who have thought very hard about this book.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power — he's going to show us the machinery underneath the sentiment.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the Oxford don's eye for character and moral imagination — a necessary counterweight.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is here as the close reader who loves this novel most fiercely and will not let us forget the verbal music underneath the argument.
Daniel, let's begin with you — because the novel sets up this collapse with something deceptively simple: the description of Tom Tulliver as a boy.
What does Eliot smuggle in under all that cream-and-roses boyishness?
The passage is a trap, and Eliot springs it with real relish.
Tom is described as utterly generic — one of those lads that grow everywhere in England, as she puts it, indistinguishable from every other pink-and-white bit of English boyhood.
And then the narrator makes her move.
She tells us that Nature has deep cunning — and that she hides her most rigid purposes precisely under those unremarkable faces.
"Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
That phrase — turned off by the gross — is a manufacturing metaphor, and I don't think it's accidental.
Tom is mass-produced English masculinity — and what is concealed inside that generic casing is precisely the instrument that will destroy Maggie.
The novel is announcing its thesis in chapter five, dressed up as a charming aside about goslings.
I think Daniel is right to flag the cunning of that passage — though I'd resist the industrial gloss.
What Eliot is describing is something far older than capitalism — it is the inscrutability of character, the fact that outward appearance is no guide to moral substance.
Tom's inflexibility is a form of integrity — a stubborn, sometimes brutal fidelity to a code.
One may not always admire the code, but one must acknowledge the character.
Johnson would have understood Tom Tulliver very well — the man who does his duty as he understands it, and pays a terrible price for the narrowness of that understanding.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the tenderness underneath the satire.
Eliot calls Maggie's face — and she says it with such affection — "poor Maggie's phiz, which Nature seemed to have moulded and coloured with the most decided intention."
The word phiz — it's colloquial, almost comic — and yet it carries all of Eliot's love for this girl.
Nature has decided something for Maggie — a distinct face, a distinct destiny — while Tom is just turned off by the gross.
That contrast is doing enormous work, and it's doing it with such lightness of touch.
That lightness is exactly what makes the economic disaster, when it comes, so devastating.
And it begins to accumulate in those chapters about Mr Tulliver's legal obsessions — his hatred of Wakem, his pride, his inability to leave well alone.
Daniel, you've been thinking about Mr Tulliver and Wakem — what does that enmity reveal about how the law actually operates in this world?
Mr Tulliver's hatred of Wakem is one of the great studies in what we might call displaced class consciousness.
Tulliver understands perfectly that the law is being used against him — that Wakem is, in his words, at the bottom of it all.
What he cannot see is that the problem isn't one malign attorney — it's the entire system in which attorneys like Wakem thrive.
And the narrator captures Tulliver's fury with devastating precision — listen to this:
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber, — always looking so sure of his game!"
The free indirect style there is extraordinary — we are inside Tulliver's outrage, but the narrator has given it a comic frame that the character cannot see.
Tulliver is right about his enemy and completely wrong about his remedy — and that contradiction is the engine of the novel's tragedy.
The portrait of Tulliver is compassionate precisely because Eliot never lets us feel entirely superior to him.
He has pride — genuine, if imprudent pride — and the novel insists that we account for that.
Consider the letter he sends to Mrs Glegg — that magnificent piece of wounded honour.
"She was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
That is not stupidity — that is a man who will not be a client to those he regards as his inferiors.
One may call it fatal imprudence, but there is something in it that commands — if not admiration — at least respect.
That letter is wonderful because it entirely wrong-foots Mrs Glegg — she's been preparing herself for magnanimity, and instead she receives defiance.
The comedy is very precise — Eliot notes that Mrs Glegg was in a state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity when the letter arrived.
That word lofty — it's doing so much work, with so little fuss.
But then I keep thinking about Mrs Tulliver in all this — because the narrator has a beautiful passage about her influence, or rather the strange way her very weakness accumulates force.
There is this extraordinary image — the feather that breaks the camel's back.
"It might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
The credit or discredit — she can't even let the poor woman have the blame cleanly.
Mrs Tulliver is not powerful — she is simply the last straw on a back already heaped with pride and obstinacy.
Caroline puts her finger on something important there — the way the novel distributes blame across a whole network of petty dominance.
Mrs Tulliver's weakness is itself a product of the same structure — she can only influence her husband by inadvertently activating his Dodson resentment.
The narrator is precise about this: whenever she departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of the Dodson family.
She is not a person to him in those moments — she is a class symbol, a cipher for everything he resents about the world above him.
And that is the mechanism by which private domestic life is infected by the class logic outside the door.
And the consequence of all that infection works its way down to the next generation — to Tom's rigidity, and to Maggie's extraordinary act of moral accusation.
Daniel, you wanted to look at what Philip Wakem's situation reveals — and then at that devastating speech of Maggie's to Tom.
Philip Wakem is the novel's most poignant figure of surplus — a person with an excess of feeling and nowhere to place it.
The narrator frames his situation with real delicacy — he wants to offer Maggie sympathy, help, nearness.
But then comes this line that stops me every time:
"There was such wealth of love in her, and there was no one to claim it all."
Wealth — claim — those are economic words, and they are not accidental.
Maggie's love is a resource that the world around her cannot receive, cannot accommodate, cannot put to use.
And Philip, for all his genuine tenderness, is also a man calculating his odds — the narrator does not let him off that hook.
You can hardly help blaming him severely, she says — and means it, even while she also means the compassion that follows.
That passage about Philip is one of the most honest things in the novel — it refuses to let him be simply the wounded romantic.
He would do anything, bear anything, for her sake — except not seeing her.
That except is everything — it reveals the one point where his devotion becomes demand.
But then you set that beside Maggie's speech to Tom, and you understand why she reaches toward Philip at all.
Because what Tom gives her is this:
"You have always enjoyed punishing me; you have always been hard and cruel to me."
She says enjoyed — not simply done — and that verb is the crux of everything.
Maggie's speech to Tom is one of the finest things in Victorian fiction — I won't pretend otherwise.
But it is also a speech made in extremis, by a young woman who has herself done wrong and who knows it.
She even concedes it in the opening breath — I know I've been wrong, often, continually.
The accusation that follows is profound, but it is also the accusation of someone arguing for her own survival.
That does not diminish it — it locates it in the human rather than the merely rhetorical.
I'd go further than Edmund.

When Maggie calls Tom a Pharisee — and reads out his entire theology of self-congratulation — she is naming something that the novel has been building toward from that very first chapter about boyish physiognomies.
She says:
"You have not even a vision of feelings by the side of which your shining virtues are mere darkness."
Shining virtues — mere darkness.
This is the novel's moral verdict on a world that rewards Tom's kind of hardness — rewards it economically, socially, legally — and calls it virtue.
Tom will succeed in business while the world that produced that success grinds Maggie into dust.
And it is no accident that Eliot gives us all of this — the pride, the law, the domestic warfare, the moral blindness — as the scaffolding for a flood that will wash the whole structure away.
We'll return after the break to look at the texture of that moral world — and what the women of St Ogg's do with it.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's great emotional centre — Maggie Tulliver herself.
And in this segment, we want to go deep into what makes her so extraordinary and so painful to read.
She is a child of ferocious intelligence in a world that has no use for it — and George Eliot watches her with something close to anguish.
With me today are three readers who know this novel intimately.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class and power — and he's particularly alive to what the system does to a mind like Maggie's.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the Oxford don's patience for character and moral texture — and a healthy suspicion of easy political readings.
And Caroline Woodcourt has been reading this novel since her teens and brings something irreplaceable — the reader's raw, unguarded response.
Let's begin in childhood — specifically with those passages where we first see Maggie's mind doing something strange and wonderful and also slightly dangerous.
What strikes me first — every time — is that the narrator doesn't just describe Maggie's mind, she performs it.
There's that extraordinary sentence about her self-taught education — let me find it.
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
That phrase — "her small mind" — is so careful and so double-edged.
It's affectionate and it's devastating at the same time.
She knows the word polygamy at eight years old — having deduced the meaning of 'poly' from the dictionary — but she has no idea gypsies aren't well supplied with groceries.
That gap is Maggie in miniature — vast reach, no map.
And that gap isn't accidental — it's the direct product of her material circumstances.
She reads the dictionary because she has so few books.
She's had one year of schooling.
This is not a story of a child who wasn't given the tools — it's a story of a child who built her own tools out of scraps, and brilliantly, and was still failed.
The narrator even tells us she is 'by no means that well trained, well-informed young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days.'
That sardonic 'necessarily' is doing real work — it's the narrator's contempt for a system that produces well-trained small females and nothing else.
Maggie's uneven, self-assembled intelligence is the novel's indictment of what her world withholds from girls.
I take Daniel's point about material circumstances, but I'd resist turning Maggie into a sociological case study.
What the narrator gives us is something far more individual — and far more comic — than a thesis about education.
The description of her thoughts as 'the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams' is a portrait of a particular human temperament.
"her thoughts generally were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams."
That is not the description of a class position — that is the description of a soul.
And it's precisely because she is constituted this way — imaginatively reckless, intellectually precocious — that she runs headlong into every wall she meets.
And the gypsy episode is where that collision becomes almost unbearably funny and sad at the same time.
She resolves to run away because Tom has rejected her — and the narrator captures that logic with such precision.
She tells us that Maggie had been told she was 'like a gypsy' and 'half wild' — so in her misery, that becomes the answer.
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
There's such a child's defiance in that exclamation mark after 'No!'
She has absorbed other people's cruelest labels and turned them into a fantasy of belonging.
It's heartbreaking and it's absurd — and somehow it's both at once.
And the fantasy collapses with extraordinary speed — which is where the Gothic comedy of the passage really ignites.
From 'very respectful companions, amenable to instruction,' the gypsies become something altogether darker in Maggie's mind.
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
'Gradual cooking' — two words that are somehow more terrifying and more comic than any direct description could be.
But look at what follows — she wonders whether the Devil, if present, would know her thoughts.
That's not comedy anymore — that's a child's theology colliding with genuine existential terror.
Eliot gives Maggie the full dignity of her fear, even while she's laughing at the situation.
What I find remarkable — and what I think Daniel's reading of class somewhat elides — is how the gypsy episode dramatises Maggie's relationship with her own imagination.
She constructs a world, inhabits it completely, and then is destroyed by her own construction.
This is the pattern of her entire life in the novel — the imagination that is her greatest gift becomes the instrument of her greatest suffering.
And notice what she most dreads, even in extremis — not death, but offending the gypsies by betraying her unfavourable opinion of them.
Even at eight years old, facing the Devil in a gypsy camp, Maggie is governed by the need to manage other people's feelings about her.
That, I think, is the deepest tragedy the novel has to offer — and it has nothing to do with the class system.
I want to go back to the scene that sets all this in motion — the moment Tom prefers Lucy, and something shifts in Maggie.
Because Eliot is so honest about it — she doesn't soften it at all.
She shows us Maggie wanting to hurt someone she loves — to slap or pinch pretty little Lucy — and she makes us understand exactly why.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse comparison — it's so precise about the particular innocence of Lucy that makes Maggie's jealousy feel almost monstrous to her.
But Eliot won't let us judge Maggie — because she also shows us exactly what Tom's unkindness has done to produce this.
The jealousy is real — and it is utterly intelligible.
And Tom's cruelty isn't incidental — it's structural.
We see it later, fully formed, in the scene where Maggie starts to defend her father before the aunts — and Tom simply shuts her down.
"'Be quiet, Maggie,' he said authoritatively, pushing her aside."
The narrator calls this 'a remarkable manifestation of self-command' — and so it is, by the novel's own standards.
But what it also is, from where I stand, is a fifteen-year-old boy learning to exercise patriarchal authority over his sister — and being praised for it.
The social order trains Tom to suppress Maggie — and he does it impeccably.
I wouldn't disagree about Tom's authority — but I think Daniel is too quick to condemn what is also genuine devotion.
The most devastating moment of this thread, for me, is not Tom's command but Mr Tulliver's farewell to his daughter.
When he says — and this is a sentence I find almost impossible to read without being moved —
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
There is no more desolate sentence in the novel.
And it falls on Maggie — who loves him utterly — with the full weight of everything she cannot fix or redeem for him.
That is what the novel is really about — love that cannot save anyone, and the people who have to go on living with that knowledge.
That sentence from Mr Tulliver — it does land like a stone.
I want to pick up on something Edmund said — about imagination as Maggie's gift and her trap — and carry it into the next part of our conversation.
Because as she grows, that imagination doesn't diminish — it intensifies, and it finds new and more dangerous objects.
We'll be turning to Maggie's adult life — and to the question of whether the novel offers her anything that isn't a form of renunciation — after a short break.

segments.title: The Comic Margins: Humor and Social Blindness

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most underappreciated qualities — its comedy.
George Eliot is not primarily thought of as a comic writer, and yet the novel is full of passages that are wickedly, precisely funny.
What's more, the comedy is never separate from the social critique — they're woven together.
Here to explore that with me are three readers I'm very glad to have in the room.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he brings a controlled fury to his readings that I find enormously clarifying.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose literary judgements are rendered with a precision that has not softened with retirement.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since girlhood and brings to it a reader's intimacy that no amount of scholarship can quite replicate.
Daniel, I want to start with you, because you've been drawn to a passage in the novel where the narrator steps back from the story and addresses the reader directly — almost polemically.
Yes — and it's one of the most remarkable passages in the whole novel, precisely because it doesn't feel like fiction at all.
Eliot is writing the history of what she calls unfashionable families, and she stops to ask: why does that history require a different tone from the one good society prefers?
And her answer is devastating.
She describes what that light irony of good society actually rests upon — and the sentence is worth reading in full.

"good society, floated on gossamer wings of light irony, is of very expensive production; requiring nothing less than a wide and arduous national life condensed in unfragrant deafening factories, cramping itself in mines, sweating at furnaces, grinding, hammering, weaving under more or less oppression of carbonic acid"
That is not a metaphor dressed up in moral clothing — that is an economic argument in novelistic prose.
The irony of the comfortable classes is literally funded by the labour of the people who can't afford irony.
And then — and this is what makes Eliot more radical than she is usually given credit for — she doesn't stop at critique.
She explains why those grinding lives require genuine belief, what she calls emphatic belief — something that gives patience and feeds human love when the limbs ache with weariness.
I won't quarrel with the eloquence of that reading, Daniel, though I'd resist calling it an economic argument.
What Eliot is doing, I think, is something far older than Marx — it is the moral tradition of noblesse oblige turned inside out.
She is not attacking property; she is attacking thoughtlessness.
The target of the satire is precisely that light and graceful irony — the incuriosity of the well-placed.
And what she defends — enthusiasm, belief, the capacity for emphasis — those are not class properties.
They are moral properties, available to the individual regardless of station.
With respect, Edmund, that reading makes the passage considerably more comfortable than it is.
Eliot lists carbonic acid and mine-work and furnace-sweat — that is not an appeal to individual moral improvement.
That is a structural indictment.
What strikes me — and I don't want to lose it in this debate — is the tenderness underneath the polemic.
Because after all that, she brings us back to Maggie.
Maggie — with her girl's face and unnoted sorrows — finding an effort and a hope that helped her through years of loneliness.
That phrase — unnoted sorrows — is so quietly painful.
And then Eliot does something that I find genuinely funny, which is to immediately show Maggie bungling her self-renunciation by being publicly, conspicuously self-denying.
She goes to the linen shop in full view of St Ogg's to ask for plain sewing — when she could have obtained it quietly.
The comedy and the compassion are completely inseparable there.
And that comic self-defeating quality in Maggie connects, I think, to a rather different kind of comedy elsewhere in the novel.
Daniel, you've also been looking at a scene involving Bob Jakin — the packman — and his extraordinary assault on Mrs Glegg.
Bob Jakin is one of the great minor characters in Victorian fiction, and this scene is a masterclass in what we might call subaltern flattery.
He's a packman — itinerant, working-class, entirely outside the property arrangements that govern everyone else in this novel.
And he deploys that position with absolute brilliance.
He flatters Mrs Glegg by attacking the shopmen — and his critique of them is also, quietly, a critique of the entire system of retail commerce that is replacing people like him.
Listen to how he puts it.

"it's a thousand pities such a lady as you shouldn't deal with a packman, i' stead o' goin' into these newfangled shops, where there's half-a-dozen fine gents wi' their chins propped up wi' a stiff stock, a-looking like bottles wi' ornamental stoppers, an' all got to get their dinner out of a bit o' calico"
Bottles with ornamental stoppers — that image is extraordinarily precise.
The shop assistant is decorative, useless, expensive — a product of commercial modernity that Bob is cheerfully, cannily dismantling.
One must admire the sheer theatrical craft of the man.
Bob Jakin is what Dr. Johnson might have called a natural rhetorician — he reads his audience with perfect accuracy and then proceeds to give her exactly what she most wishes to hear.
Mrs Glegg, after all, has spent her entire life convinced that she sees through people — and here is Bob confirming it.
He even says — you can see through them shopmen, I'll be bound — as though Mrs Glegg's penetrating intelligence were itself the point of the transaction.
I would resist Daniel's class-war framing here — this is really about individual wit and individual vanity meeting in the market.
I think the comedy here is also about gender, actually — and Eliot is fully in on the joke.
Bob leads with Mrs Glegg's figure — Mumps is particularly fond of ladies with good shapes.
It's outrageous, and Mrs Glegg — who is habitually impervious to charm — is apparently not entirely unmoved.
What Eliot is showing us is that everyone has a vanity Bob Jakin can find — and that finding it is a kind of democratic genius.
But of course the novel also contains humour of a much darker, more savage kind.
Daniel, you've been looking at two passages involving Tom — one where he confronts Philip Wakem, and one where he finally casts Maggie out.
What Tom Tulliver represents, in these two passages, is the ideology of respectability taken to its logical and brutal conclusion.
The confrontation with Philip is genuinely chilling — and it uses the language of mockery with horrifying precision.
Tom tells Philip exactly what the social world thinks of a disabled man aspiring to love.
"I'll thrash you; I'll hold you up to public scorn. Who wouldn't laugh at the idea of your turning lover to a fine girl?"
That question — who wouldn't laugh — is the cruelest possible deployment of social consensus as a weapon.
Tom is not expressing a personal opinion; he is invoking the laughter of the crowd — of good society — as an instrument of annihilation.
And then, against Maggie, he's even more absolute.

"You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father's name. You have been a curse to your best friends. You have been base, deceitful; no motives are strong enough to restrain you. I wash my hands of you forever. You don't belong to me."
Each sentence is a hammer blow — the repetition of you have is almost liturgical, and the ritual is excommunication.
Tom is not a villain, and I think it's a mistake to read him as one.
He is a man of severely limited moral imagination — but his limitations are entirely coherent.
He has absorbed the ethic of his class and station and applies it with complete consistency.
The tragedy — and it is a tragedy — is that a code of honour which functions adequately in the world of commerce is catastrophically inadequate for the world of feeling.
That is not class ideology — that is the ancient problem of the person who does not know what they do not know.
What strikes me about both those Tom passages is that Eliot never lets us simply condemn him.

Even in the linen shop scene earlier, she says of Tom's rebuke — and this stopped me on re-reading — that there was some tenderness and bravery mingled with the worldliness and self-assertion of that little speech.
She holds both things simultaneously — his cruelty and his love — and refuses to let us drop either one.
That is not comedy, exactly — but it is the same quality of vision that makes the comedy work.
The ability to see a person whole, even when they are doing something terrible.
And that wholeness of vision — seeing people clearly without despising them — brings us, I think, to Philip's letter to Maggie, which Caroline has been looking at.
Because here we have a character who has been mocked, dismissed, threatened — and who responds with something that is the exact opposite of everything Tom represents.
Philip's letter is — I find it almost unbearable to read.
Not because it is sentimental — it isn't — but because it is so astonishingly generous in the teeth of real pain.
And it contains a sentence that I think is the finest in the novel.
"You have been to my affections what light, what colour is to my eyes, what music is to the inward ear, you have raised a dim unrest into a vivid consciousness."
The accumulation of that sentence — light, colour, music, the inward ear — builds and builds, and then it lands on that phrase: a dim unrest into a vivid consciousness.
That is what art does, and what love does — it makes the world more real.
And Philip — who Tom has just called puny and miserable and publicly ridiculous — is the one who says it.
What I find significant is the contrast Philip himself draws — between his love for Maggie and Stephen's attraction to her.
He describes Stephen's pull on Maggie as belonging to that partial, divided action of our nature which makes half the tragedy of the human lot.
That is Philip understanding, with terrible clarity, that passion can coexist with a fundamental incompatibility of soul.
And that understanding — that generous, agonising understanding — is precisely what Tom is constitutionally incapable of.
Philip's letter is, to my mind, the moral centre of the novel — and it is the more remarkable for being so unheroic in its circumstances.
He is writing from physical pain, from jealousy, from loss — and he chooses, deliberately, to place Maggie's welfare above every one of those claims.
That is not sentiment — that is what the moral tradition calls virtue, achieved at cost.
I am glad, for once, to find myself in agreement with my colleague.
That rare moment of consensus seems like an excellent place to pause.
We've moved today from the comedy of Bob Jakin's magnificent salesmanship, through the chilling social laughter that Tom deploys as a weapon, to the luminous generosity of Philip's letter.
What the novel keeps insisting is that the capacity for real feeling — for emphasis, to use Eliot's own word — is not equally distributed.
Some have it ground out of them by necessity; some are insulated from it by comfort; and a very few — like Philip — have it refined by suffering into something extraordinary.
We'll be back shortly with more from The Mill on the Floss.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today's close reading focuses on siblings — the intricate, sometimes brutal bond between Maggie and Tom Tulliver.
We're looking at moments where George Eliot opens the novel's deepest questions: about childhood suffering, about gendered judgment, about who gets to belong.
With me today are three voices who know this novel intimately.
Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of classic fiction — someone who first met Maggie as a teenager and has never quite recovered.
Dr Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomy lessons in class power — he will not let us forget who the system rewards and who it destroys.
And Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don, who believes the novel's real business is moral imagination — character tested by the world.
Let's begin with childhood — and with what George Eliot insists we stop dismissing.
There's a passage early on — after Maggie has cut off her own hair in one of those rash, desperate acts — where the narrator turns and addresses the reader almost reproachfully.
She's standing crying before the glass, surrounded by her shorn locks, and Eliot compares her to Ajax among the slaughtered sheep — which is both comic and genuinely moving.
But then the narrator steps back and makes this extraordinary claim about the seriousness of children's pain.

"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships; but it was not less bitter to Maggie—perhaps it was even more bitter—than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
That phrase — "the real troubles of mature life" — Eliot uses it with such delicate irony, that little word "antithetically."
She's saying: we invented that hierarchy between childhood pain and adult pain, and we invented it to protect ourselves from memory.
What strikes me is how much of that passage is written in the first-person plural — "we have all of us sobbed," "we can no longer recall."
Eliot is not merely defending Maggie — she is indicting the reader.
She is asking: have you, comfortable adult, truly forgotten what it was to be small and helpless and laughed at?
That is, at its core, a moral argument — and a remarkably confident one.
It is the kind of argument that Johnson would have recognised: the appeal to common experience as the ground of ethical judgment.
I'd press that a little further, Edmund.
Notice the structural contrast Eliot draws between Maggie and Tom in the same passage.
Tom has a wonderful instinctive discernment of what would turn to his advantage or disadvantage — and so his mother hardly ever calls him naughty.
Tom's social legibility — his knack for appearing correct — protects him.
Maggie's passionate impulse makes her perpetually visible in the wrong way.
That asymmetry is not a character flaw — it is the architecture of a society that will later, as adults, destroy her while elevating him.
And the comic passages about Tom are wonderful precisely because they complicate that picture.
There's this marvellous scene where Tom has disguised himself — burnt cork eyebrows, red turban, scarf, sword — trying desperately to look terrifying.
And Eliot gives us this perfectly observed detail.
"Philip had once told him of a man who had a horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a horseshoe on his forehead."
There is something utterly disarming about that — the earnestness of it, the effort.
Tom, who will become rigid and punitive, is here just a boy desperately practicing his face in the mirror.
That is precisely where Eliot's moral imagination is at its finest — she will not give us villains.
Tom is limited, yes — even cruel in certain moments — but Eliot remembers always that he was once a boy frowning at himself in a glass, longing to be fearsome.
The same compassion she extends to Maggie, she extends to Tom — even when Tom does not extend it to his sister.
That asymmetry of compassion within the narrative is what makes the novel, I think, genuinely painful rather than merely polemical.
There's a passage I want to bring in here — Tom at school, under Mr Stelling, broken down by lessons he cannot master.
Eliot tells us that under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before.
It's a shocking phrase — and worth sitting with.
Tom reduced to helplessness acquires what Eliot calls "the girl's susceptibility" — as though susceptibility and femininity are interchangeable.
Eliot is being culturally precise, not endorsing the equivalence — she is showing us what that world believes.
And then comes this devastating detail — Tom, at his lowest, resorting to prayer.
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
The gap between the register of prayer and the content of that petition is where Eliot locates all the pathos of a boy crushed by an institution built for other boys.
And he prays for Euclid too — he's not sure how to frame it, whether to ask to understand it or to be rid of it.
In the end he settles for: make Mr Stelling say I sha'n't do Euclid any more.
It's funny — genuinely funny — and also quite heartbreaking, because this is the same Tom who will later show no such flexibility toward Maggie.
The boy who prayed for mercy received none from his institution — and grew up unable to offer it.
Which brings us to what that same society does to Maggie when she is grown.
The passages from chapter fifty-five are, I think, among the most ferocious things Eliot ever wrote.
Caroline — you've written about the voice Eliot uses here.
Yes — and it's a voice quite unlike anything else in the novel.
Eliot invents this character — "the world's wife" — who speaks for respectable opinion, for the herd consensus that judges Maggie.
And the satire is almost savage in its precision.
Listen to this.
"The world's wife, with that fine instinct which is given her for the preservation of Society, saw at once that Miss Tulliver's conduct had been of the most aggravated kind."
That phrase — "fine instinct" — doing the work that "spite" and "cruelty" and "cowardice" might otherwise do.
Eliot gives the world's wife her own grammar of self-congratulation — and then lets the reader watch it operate on an innocent woman.
What's clinching, to me, is the cameo Tom receives in that passage.
The world's wife approves of Tom — "a truly respectable young man, Mr Tom Tulliver; quite likely to rise in the world."
Tom's cruelty to his sister is reframed as moral seriousness — as evidence of his good character.
His sister's disgrace is a heavy blow to him — the language is almost sympathetic toward the man who turned her from his door.
That is how ideological systems reproduce themselves: by rewarding those who enforce the rules and mourning their burden in doing so.
I wouldn't dispute the diagnosis — but I find the more troubling detail to be the line about God.
Eliot ends that catalogue of social viciousness with a quiet parenthesis: He had not the care of society on His hands, as the world's wife had.
The irony is devastating — God, being merely divine, lacks the ruthlessness required to manage respectability.
It is, in miniature, a complete portrait of what organised piety becomes when it serves social hierarchy rather than moral truth.
And against all of that — Maggie's response.
She has every reason to flee — and yet she refuses.
She says — and Eliot marks it carefully, "with some of the old proud fire flashing out" —
"I will not go away because people say false things of me. They shall learn to retract them."
"The old proud fire." Eliot is recalling everything we have seen of Maggie from childhood — the passionate impulse, the refusal to simply submit.
It's also a moment of terrible irony — because we know, as readers, that they won't retract them.
The world's wife is not in the business of retracting.
What I find remarkable is that phrase — "I should feel like a lonely wanderer, cut off from the past."
For Maggie, St Ogg's — for all its cruelty — is her past, her memory, her family.
The community that is destroying her is also the only community she has.
That is an extraordinarily precise description of what economic and social dependence actually does to a person — it makes exile from the place that harms you feel like self-annihilation.
And yet — I think one must also read that passage as a moment of genuine moral courage, not only structural entrapment.
Maggie says she wishes to atone to Lucy — to those she has hurt — before she considers her own comfort.
That is not the reasoning of a victim; that is the reasoning of someone with a clear moral account of what she owes and to whom.
Eliot gives Maggie, even at her lowest, the dignity of someone who takes ethics seriously — more seriously, one might add, than anyone around her.
So we end this segment with Maggie standing her ground — the child who cut her hair and wept among the black locks now a woman refusing to be driven from her own life.
There's a thread running through all of these passages — from the child's anguish to the adult's defiance — that Eliot refuses to let us cut.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's treatment of education — what it gives, what it withholds, and who decides.

segments.title: Estrangement and Atmosphere: The Widening Breach

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

Today we're exploring one of the novel's most emotionally charged preoccupations: the widening breach between Maggie and Tom, and the atmosphere of suffering that gathers around Maggie in the later books.
With me are three readers who have thought about this novel long and hard.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings a scholar's sensitivity to character and moral imagination — and a willingness to defend the novel's emotional ambitions on their own terms.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Eliot's world as a system — and asks what the novel reveals about who bears the cost of that system.
And Caroline Woodcourt is our close reader — someone who came to this novel young and has never quite left it.
Edmund, let's begin with you — with that shattering early moment when news of the family's ruin reaches the children.
Thank you — and this passage is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating in the entire novel.
What Eliot does here is refuse to sentimentalise the children's grief.
Maggie weeps — of course she does — but the real literary event is Tom's inability to weep.
He feels what the narrator calls the pressure of the heart which forbids tears — that is not numbness.
That is a particular and terrible form of suffering that closes a person inward rather than releasing them.
And then Eliot offers us what I consider one of her finest similes in the whole book.
"He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank, — as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path."
That image — a black curtain of cloud falling on a path — is not decorative.
It anticipates the whole of Tom's subsequent character: the man who cannot see beyond the immediate obstruction, who cannot weep and therefore cannot forgive.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the physical detail: the arm tightened almost convulsively.
Tom does love Maggie — in this moment, it's absolutely there in his body — and yet already his face is a closed door.
Eliot gives us the tragedy of Tom in miniature right here.
His love is real, but it cannot flow outward — it calcifies.
And Maggie, who weeps freely, is already the more open — and therefore the more vulnerable — of the two.
Precisely so.
And I'd add that Eliot is entirely fair to Tom in this passage.
She doesn't render his rigidity as cruelty — not here.
She shows us that it is a form of weight-bearing — the masculine posture that misfortune imposes and which then becomes permanent character.
I'd agree that the passage is remarkable — though I want to press on where that rigidity comes from.
Tom has no distinct vision of their troubles, the narrator tells us — he only feels the crushing weight of what seemed unmitigated misfortune.
That blankness isn't simply psychology — it's the condition of a boy who has been prepared by his culture to act, not to understand.
The same novel shows us, a little later, Tom in his small lodgings with his large ambitions — and Eliot turns the narrator on him with a kind of amused sympathy.
There's a passage where Maggie retreats laughing from Tom flicking a bell-rope, and the narrator takes the opportunity to address the reader directly.

"not very far either, — a touch of human experience which I flatter myself will come home to the bosoms of not a few substantial or distinguished men who were once at an early stage of their rise in the world, and were cherishing very large hopes in very small lodgings."
That irony is corrosive if you let it be.
Tom's drive to restore the family name is also the ideology of petit-bourgeois respectability — and Eliot knows it, even as she warms to him.
That address to the reader is one of my favourite moments of authorial mischief in the whole novel.
She's flattering the men in her readership — and gently puncturing them at the same time.
But what I notice is that Maggie is already retreating — laughing, yes, but retreating.
Even in the comic passages, Eliot plants the seed of what's coming — Maggie making herself smaller around Tom.
Daniel's reading of Tom is shrewd, though I think one must be careful not to reduce him to a social type.
Tom is also a young man who takes responsibility — who actually restores what his father lost.
The novel gives him credit for that — as it should.
The tragedy is not that Tom is a vehicle of ideology — it is that his virtues and his failures are the same quality of character.
That's a fair point — and I'd concede it, up to a degree.
But when we get to the later books and watch what Tom's judgment does to Maggie — then I find it harder to be generous.
Consider the passage after Tom has cast her out.

"The idea of ever recovering happiness never glimmered in her mind for a moment; it seemed as if every sensitive fibre in her were too entirely preoccupied by pain ever to vibrate again to another influence."
Every sensitive fibre — preoccupied by pain — unable to vibrate to another influence.
Eliot is describing a woman whose capacity for life has been crushed — not by fate, but by a specific human being exercising a specific social authority over her.
And that authority — a brother's right to pronounce on a sister's honour — is not natural.
That passage undoes me every time.
Life stretched before her as one act of penitence — and she isn't even certain she did wrong.
What haunts her is her own weakness — the possibility that she might fall again.
Eliot understands that the cruellest suffering is not punishment from outside — it's the self-accusation that has been so thoroughly internalised it feels like conscience.
And yet — and this is what keeps me reading — Maggie is not broken.
She still reaches toward connection.
Which brings us to Philip Wakem — and one of the most charged small scenes in the book.
Bob brings Maggie a letter — no postmark — in a handwriting she knows intimately.
Eliot tells us that Maggie recognises the hand in which her name had been written long ago in a pocket Shakespeare she possesses.
"a hand in which her name had been written long ago, in a pocket Shakespeare which she possessed."
That pocket Shakespeare — it carries the whole weight of their clandestine friendship, the library meetings, the reading together.
And then Maggie — in violent agitation — hurries upstairs to be alone with it.
The mother is in the room.
That single detail — the surveillance of the domestic space — tells you everything about why Maggie's inner life must always be conducted in hiding.
I find that reading of surveillance rather forced, if I may say so.
Mrs Tulliver is simply present — as mothers are.
What interests me is the pocket Shakespeare — that is the image of genuine tenderness between two young people who found each other through books.
And she reads the letter with a throbbing brow — that is the body's response to love that has been suppressed and then suddenly reinstated.
Eliot understands the physiology of longing — it is one of her great gifts as a novelist.
I think both of you are right — and that's why the scene works as well as it does.
The pocket Shakespeare is a beautiful private symbol — and the mother in the room is a real constraint.
Eliot is always working on both levels simultaneously — the inner life and the world that presses on it.
What's so remarkable about these passages taken together is how Eliot sustains the emotional logic across books — the same characters, deepening and hardening.
Tom's blank eyes in childhood — those large hopes in small lodgings — and finally Maggie, pain preoccupying every fibre.
The breach between them widens not through any single dramatic rupture but through the slow, inexorable logic of who each of them has become.
We'll return after the break to look more closely at that final estrangement — and what the novel asks us to feel about it.

segments.title: Closing: The Flood and What It Takes

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the currents that run through The Mill on the Floss — memory, class, conscience, the grinding weight of family obligation.
And now we come to the close — which is also, in a sense, where the novel began.
Edmund, I want to start with you — because the novel opens with one of the most unusual narrative gambits in Victorian fiction.
Yes — and it's a gambit that rewards the most careful attention on a second or third reading.
The narrator begins in what feels like pure, unmediated vision — the mill, the river, the frost.
And then — quite suddenly — she pulls the rug from beneath us.
She says, and I must read this precisely:

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
The entire opening — the river, the mill, that girl with the dark hair — was a reverie.
Memory, not observation. Longing, not presence.
And that, to my mind, is the key to everything that follows — the whole novel is saturated in retrospective grief.
That moment never loses its power, no matter how many times you've read it.
You feel the physical detail — elbows pressing into armrests — and it's so bodily, so domestic.
And then you understand: this tenderness for Dorlcote Mill is the tenderness of someone who can never go back.
The flood at the end of the novel takes everything — but George Eliot is telling us from the very first page that loss is the novel's very element.
I'd agree — but I want to press on what is actually lost, and for whom.
Because this novel is also a sustained anatomy of what the system does to its most passionate and intelligent members when they refuse to conform.
And Maggie's suffering isn't simply personal tragedy — it's structural.
Consider the passage where Tom drags Maggie away from Philip in the Red Deeps.

"Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience and her deepest dread; she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the character he had given to her conduct, and yet her whole soul rebelled against it as unfair from its incompleteness."
That word — incompleteness — is doing enormous work.
Tom's moral verdict on Maggie is true in a narrow, rigid sense — and entirely false in every sense that matters.
I don't resist that reading, though I'd frame it differently.
What George Eliot gives us in Tom is something far more troubling than a villain — she gives us a man of complete moral sincerity whose sincerity is utterly blind.
The narrator tells us plainly:

"Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them."
That is not satire — that is tragic irony of the highest order.
A man who causes devastation while certain he is doing right — that is one of literature's great and terrible portraits.
And the cruelty of the scene in the Red Deeps is that Tom's worst words are aimed not just at Maggie but through her at Philip.
He says — and I find this passage almost unbearable — he says:
"I'll save her from throwing herself away on you,—from making herself a laughing-stock,—from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son."
Not good enough for his son.
Tom deploys the very class logic he affects to despise — to wound Philip with his own father's contempt.
It's devastating. And it's devastatingly true to how people actually use each other's vulnerabilities.
Exactly — and this connects to the passage about Tom and Philip's schoolboy friendship, which the narrator dissects with surgical precision.
There's a line about the impossibility of certain friendships that I think resonates across the entire novel.
"If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out."
That image of incompatible metals — it's not just about Tom and Philip.
It describes every relationship in the novel that class and pride and the weight of the past make finally impossible.
That image of welding and metal is one of the great figures in George Eliot — scientific in its precision, tragic in its implication.
And what it suggests, I think, is that character — formed early, formed deep — is not readily remade by circumstances or affection.
The flood at the end does not redeem — it simply overwhelms.
Tom and Maggie are briefly, terribly reconciled in the moment before drowning — but that reconciliation is possible only because everything else has been swept away.
And that is why the narrator's opening reverie matters so much at the close.
The novel begins in the warmth of remembered belonging — pressing elbows into an armchair, dreaming of Dorlcote Mill.
And it ends by drowning everything that was dreamed of.
George Eliot knew — from experience, from loss — that you can love a place and a life so completely that its ending feels like the ending of the world.
And on that note — which feels exactly right — we bring this episode to a close.
The Mill on the Floss asks us to hold together things that resist each other — love and resentment, memory and loss, the pull of family and the cost of belonging.
My thanks to Daniel Rosen, Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that was, I think, worthy of the novel.
We'll be back with another episode of The Mill on the Floss Unpacked very soon.

c14:p2.text:
Mr Stelling was a well-sized, broad-chested man, not yet thirty, with flaxen
hair standing erect, and large lightish-gray eyes, which were always very wide
open; he had a sonorous bass voice, and an air of defiant self-confidence
inclining to brazenness. He had entered on his career with great vigor, and
intended to make a considerable impression on his fellow-men. The Rev. Walter
Stelling was not a man who would remain among the “inferior clergy”
all his life. He had a true British determination to push his way in the
world,—as a schoolmaster, in the first place, for there were capital
masterships of grammar-schools to be had, and Mr Stelling meant to have one of
them; but as a preacher also, for he meant always to preach in a striking
manner, so as to have his congregation swelled by admirers from neighbouring
parishes, and to produce a great sensation whenever he took occasional duty for
a brother clergyman of minor gifts. The style of preaching he had chosen was
the extemporaneous, which was held little short of the miraculous in rural
parishes like King’s Lorton. Some passages of Massillon and Bourdaloue,
which he knew by heart, were really very effective when rolled out in Mr
Stelling’s deepest tones; but as comparatively feeble appeals of his own
were delivered in the same loud and impressive manner, they were often thought
quite as striking by his hearers. Mr Stelling’s doctrine was of no
particular school; if anything, it had a tinge of evangelicalism, for that was
“the telling thing” just then in the diocese to which King’s
Lorton belonged. In short, Mr Stelling was a man who meant to rise in his
profession, and to rise by merit, clearly, since he had no interest beyond what
might be promised by a problematic relationship to a great lawyer who had not
yet become Lord Chancellor. A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions
naturally gets a little into debt at starting; it is not to be expected that he
will live in the meagre style of a man who means to be a poor curate all his
life; and if the few hundreds Mr Timpson advanced toward his daughter’s
fortune did not suffice for the purchase of handsome furniture, together with a
stock of wine, a grand piano, and the laying out of a superior flower-garden,
it followed in the most rigorous manner, either that these things must be
procured by some other means, or else that the Rev. Mr Stelling must go
without them, which last alternative would be an absurd procrastination of the
fruits of success, where success was certain. Mr Stelling was so broad-chested
and resolute that he felt equal to anything; he would become celebrated by
shaking the consciences of his hearers, and he would by and by edit a Greek
play, and invent several new readings. He had not yet selected the play, for
having been married little more than two years, his leisure time had been much
occupied with attentions to Mrs Stelling; but he had told that fine woman what
he meant to do some day, and she felt great confidence in her husband, as a man
who understood everything of that sort.
c14:p2.summary: Rev. Stelling is an ambitious, pretentious clergyman determined to rise in his profession through impressive preaching and scholarly pursuits, despite lacking genuine depth or means.
c14:p2.best_quote: A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting

c25:p73.text:
Their mother came in now, and Maggie rushed away, that her burst of tears,
which she felt must come, might not happen till she was safe upstairs. They
were very bitter tears; everybody in the world seemed so hard and unkind to
Maggie; there was no indulgence, no fondness, such as she imagined when she
fashioned the world afresh in her own thoughts. In books there were people who
were always agreeable or tender, and delighted to do things that made one
happy, and who did not show their kindness by finding fault. The world outside
the books was not a happy one, Maggie felt; it seemed to be a world where
people behaved the best to those they did not pretend to love, and that did not
belong to them. And if life had no love in it, what else was there for Maggie?
Nothing but poverty and the companionship of her mother’s narrow griefs,
perhaps of her father’s heart-cutting childish dependence. There is no
hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants,
and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we
who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the
future lightened the blind sufferer’s present.
c25:p73.summary: Maggie rushes upstairs with bitter tears, feeling the world is hard and unkind; the narrator reveals her anguish: she expected love and tenderness from others as she imagines from books, but finds a harsh world where affection shows itself as fault-finding, and she sees no hope without love.

c37:p91.text:
Maggie went up to her own room to pour out all that indignant remonstrance,
against which Tom’s mind was close barred, in bitter tears. Then, when
the first burst of unsatisfied anger was gone by, came the recollection of that
quiet time before the pleasure which had ended in to-day’s misery had
perturbed the clearness and simplicity of her life. She used to think in that
time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene
heights above worldly temptations and conflict. And here she was down again in
the thick of a hot strife with her own and others’ passions. Life was not
so short, then, and perfect rest was not so near as she had dreamed when she
was two years younger. There was more struggle for her, and perhaps more
falling. If she had felt that she was entirely wrong, and that Tom had been
entirely right, she could sooner have recovered more inward harmony; but now
her penitence and submission were constantly obstructed by resentment that
would present itself to her no otherwise than as a just indignation. Her heart
bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him
with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost
like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and
tighten her fingers on her palm.
c37:p91.summary: Maggie pours out her indignation in tears; she recalls her earlier spiritual peace and recognises that she has fallen again into worldly conflict. Her penitence is constantly obstructed by resentment at Tom's cruelty toward Philip; her empathy for Philip's suffering is acute and physically painful, causing her to beat the floor in distress.
